name: Columba
knownFor: Irish monk who left Ireland for good as a pilgrim for Christ, founded the monastery on Iona, and left heirs who led a family of houses in Britain and Ireland, sent Aidan to the English and defended his Easter custom at Whitby.
dates: Sixth century. Sailed to Britain in his forty-second year, two years after the battle of Cooldrevny, in Adomnán's words: 562 in the Irish and Welsh annals, 565 in Bede's, about 563 in Wentworth Huyshe's reckoning. Died in June, in 597 by the usual reckoning; the Annals of Ulster give 9 June, under 594, in his seventy-sixth year, and Bede says he died at seventy-seven. Huyshe gives his years as 521 to 597
place: Ireland by birth, where he founded Durrow; Iona, a small island off northern Britain, in what is now Scotland, from which he went among the Picts
role: Monk; founder and abbot of Iona

traces: Bede says many monasteries in Britain and Ireland had their beginning through his disciples, from Iona and from the house he built in Ireland before he sailed, the Field of Oaks, Durrow, and that the Iona house was the chief of them all. Baithene succeeded him as abbot, and later abbots of Iona are called his heirs in the Annals of Ulster.
Bede says the abbot of Iona, a priest, ruled the whole province, even its bishops, after the example of Columba, who was a priest and monk and not a bishop.
In 635 Oswald, king of Northumbria, asked the elders of the Irish for a bishop and was sent Aidan, "a monk of the island called Hii", Iona.
Iona kept his way of dating Easter until 716, Bede says, when it took up the Roman reckoning; Bede also gives 715.
remembered: Bede calls him a famous priest and abbot, a monk by habit and life. He is unsure what kind of man Columba was, but sure that he left successors known for self-control, the love of God and life under a rule.
Adomnán, ninth abbot of Iona, wrote his Life about a century after him, and says his name reached beyond Ireland and Britain to Spain, Gaul, Italy and Rome itself.

At the synod Bede places at Streaneshalch, Whitby, in 664, Colman, the bishop from Iona's line, defended "our most reverend Father Columba and his successors"; Wilfrid, the priest who spoke for the Roman side, granted he might be a holy man and asked whether he could be preferred to Peter. King Oswy ruled for Rome.

uncertain: His life comes from Adomnán, abbot of Iona, who wrote about a hundred years after Columba died. Wentworth Huyshe says Adomnán was born twenty-seven years after Columba's death and probably wrote the Life between his visits to Ireland in 692 and 697. Adomnán says he wrote from older writings and from what faithful old men told him. He writes as Columba's successor, and arranges the Life by kinds of wonder: prophecies, miracles and visions. Columba's sayings in it are Adomnán's report. No writing by Columba and no witness from his lifetime is held.
Bede, an English monk who finished his history in 731, wrote as a critic of Iona's Easter custom and for the side that won at Whitby.

The year he came to Britain. Adomnán gives his forty-second year, two years after the battle of Cooldrevny, which the Annals of Ulster enter under both 559 and 560. The Annals of Ulster and the Annales Cambriae put the voyage in 562. Bede gives 565, in the ninth year of Bridius, king of the Picts; Huyshe, dating Bridius's reign from 554, makes it 563.

His years and age. Huyshe gives 521 to 597, and 597 is the usual modern date. The Annals of Ulster put his death under 594, in his seventy-sixth year, and again, as an alternative, under 600. Bede says he died at seventy-seven, about thirty-two years after he came to Britain. The Annales Cambriae record his birth in a year their editor, John Williams ab Ithel, sets at 521, and his death in their year 151, which on the same count falls in 595. The Middle Irish Life in the Book of Lismore, a late text, gives seventy-seven years and forty-five in Scotland. Whitley Stokes reports that the birthday the Book of Lismore Life gives, a Thursday, 7 December, points to 517 or 523, but Bishop William Reeves thinks 521 most likely.

Why he left Ireland. Adomnán gives only his wish "to make a pilgrimage for Christ", and names the battle of Cooldrevny only to date the voyage. Huyshe's introduction gives the battle as the cause "according to tradition" and counts the tales around his exile as legends. Adomnán does tell of a synod at Teltown that excommunicated Columba, wrongly as it later proved, for causes no source gives. Huyshe thinks it possibly met in 561, after the battle.
Who gave him Iona. Bede says the Picts gave him the island. The Annals of Ulster say Conall, son of Comgall, granted it.

How far he converted the Picts. Bede says he turned the northern Picts to the faith by his preaching and example. Adomnán tells of King Brude's gates opening of their own accord, a wonder in his voice, and of the king honouring him for life, and of a countryman with his household and an old chief baptized through an interpreter. He never says the king or the nation was baptized.

The day of his death. Adomnán puts it in the night after a Saturday, soon after a day in May when he blessed the island. The Annals of Ulster give 9 June. The Book of Lismore Life says the night of Pentecost Sunday.

Later tradition credits him with books, among them the Cathach and the Book of Durrow, and with poems and hymns. For the Latin hymn Altus Prosator, Huyshe reports the Marquess of Bute's view that the ascription rests on an apparently unbroken tradition. These rest on Huyshe's introduction; no early source here says so.

briefReferences: Adomnán, Life of Saint Columba, Book III, tr. Wentworth Huyshe: his last day, the Psalter, "they that seek the Lord shall not want any good thing", and Baithene to write what follows; his last words, heard by Diormit alone; the midnight bell, the altar, and the hand raised to bless.

Adomnán, second preface: born of noble parentage; the voyage in his forty-second year, two years after the battle, "to make a pilgrimage for Christ"; never an hour without prayer, reading, writing or work.
Adomnán, Book III: twelve disciples sailed with him.
Adomnán, Book II: King Brude's gates opening "of their own accord", and the king's lasting honour.
Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.4: Durrow before the voyage; he turned the northern Picts to the faith; Iona the chief of his houses; the abbot over bishops; "whatsoever he was himself".
Bede III.3: Aidan, a monk of Iona, sent to Oswald in 635.
Bede III.25: the synod at Whitby, 664; Colman's defence of "our most reverend Father Columba and his successors"; the king's ruling.
Bede III.4 and V.22: Iona kept its custom until 715 or 716.
Annals of Ulster and Annales Cambriae: 562 for the voyage; Huyshe: about 563, and 597 for the death.
World census, Insular / Irish Monastic Christianity: his setting; a church led by abbots rather than city bishops.

quotationOriginals.modern: My sons, I entrust these last words to you. Love one another without pretence, and live in peace.
quotationOriginals.printed: These my last words I commend to you, O my sons, that ye have mutual and unfeigned charity among yourselves, with peace
quotationOriginals.work: Adomnán, Life of Saint Columba, Book III, tr. Wentworth Huyshe
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Adomnán's Latin is not held; rendered from Huyshe's English. "Charity" is rendered "love", since its modern sense misleads. The sentence goes on with a promise, cut here.

quotationOriginals.modern: But whatever kind of man he was, this much about him we hold as certain. He left successors known for great self-control, for the love of God, and for life under a rule.
quotationOriginals.printed: But whatsoever he was himself, this we know for certain, that he left successors renowned for their continency, their love of God, and observance of monastic rules.
